analysis.one_liner: Bans internet providers from charging websites for faster lanes or favoring their own services.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote; it sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and one of its subcommittees until the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the FCC to write rules banning "paid prioritization" — broadband providers charging websites or services extra for faster, smoother delivery to users. It would also ban internet providers from speeding up their own content or a partner's content ahead of competitors. The FCC would have had 90 days after passage to issue the rules, with fines for violations under the Communications Act. [S2] [S3]
analysis.who_benefits: Everyday internet users, who keep a level playing field where websites and services compete on quality rather than on who can pay the provider for a fast lane; and smaller websites, startups, and streaming services that could not afford priority fees.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Internet users and small online businesses

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits broadband providers from agreeing to give any website or app faster or preferential treatment in exchange for payment — the practice known as paid prioritization. [S2] [S3]
Prohibits broadband providers from favoring their own content, apps, services, or devices — or those of an affiliate — over competitors' traffic. [S2] [S3]
Keeps emergency communications, law enforcement, public safety, and national security traffic unaffected, so the ban does not interfere with those needs. [S3]
Gives the FCC enforcement authority with fines, while preserving its broader authority to write open-internet rules in the pending GN Docket No. 14-28 proceeding. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Broadband providers — cable and telephone companies — lose the ability to charge edge providers for priority delivery or to steer users toward their own services. Providers also argued the ban could reduce revenue that helps fund network investment.

drawbacks.text: Broadband providers argued that fees for priority traffic could help fund network upgrades, and that a blanket ban removes one possible revenue source for building capacity. [S3]
The bill requires the FCC to issue the rules within 90 days of enactment, a very short window for a major rulemaking, which providers and other critics could argue produces a rushed record. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary internet users the benefits are straightforward: the bill would keep the internet a flat market where every site loads at the speed your connection allows, rather than one where deep-pocketed companies buy faster delivery and everyone else gets the leftover capacity. The cost falls almost entirely on broadband providers, who would give up a potential revenue stream; the honest counterargument is that network investment relies partly on such revenue, though providers could still sell more capacity to everyone and the bill preserves legitimate traffic management for safety and security. Notably, the FCC went on to ban paid prioritization through its own open-internet rules in 2015, and later Republican-majority FCCs rolled those rules back, so the underlying fight continued after this bill died.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to a subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended with no markup, no floor vote, and no action. [S5]

narrative.text: Rep. Doris Matsui introduced the bill on June 17, 2014, with Reps. Henry Waxman and Anna Eshoo joining as original sponsors. [S1] [S3]
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce. [S5]
Three days later, on June 20, 2014, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade. [S5]
No further action was ever taken; the bill received ten cosponsors, all Democrats, and died at the end of the 113th Congress without a committee vote or a floor vote. [S4] [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Broadband providers, who faced no ban on selling priority access or favoring their own services; the bill's supporters got nothing from the outcome.

for.name: Rep. Doris Matsui
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill directing the FCC to ban paid prioritization and self-preferencing by broadband providers. [S1] [S3]

for.name: Reps. Henry Waxman and Anna Eshoo
for.what_they_did: Joined Matsui in introducing the bill on the day it was filed. [S3]

for.name: 10 of 201 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on. [S4]

against.name: Rep. Fred Upton
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Committee under his chairmanship referred the bill to a subcommittee and never scheduled a markup or sent it to the floor; it died there. [S5]

against.name: Broadband providers (cable and telephone companies)
against.what_they_did: Opposed net-neutrality legislation in this period, arguing paid priority arrangements and self-preferencing should remain lawful; no hearing or vote on this bill ever occurred. [S5]

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all ten cosponsors were Democrats, and the Republican-run Energy and Commerce Committee took no action; the bill never reached a floor vote, so no roll-call split exists. [S4] [S5]

industries.note: The bill would have banned them from charging websites for faster delivery and from favoring their own apps and services over competitors'. Their interest in selling 'fast lanes' runs against internet users' interest in a level playing field, since the cost of priority fees ultimately shapes what users see and what startups can afford. [S2] [S3]

industries.industry: Edge providers (websites, streaming services, startups, app makers)
industries.note: The bill would have protected them from having to pay for priority delivery or compete against their own internet provider's favored services. Their interest in equal-speed access lines up directly with internet users'. [S3]
